events.text: The council gathers. Mission 1 begins.
Elena proposes Elena, Omar. I know I am Good, and there is no evidence yet to distinguish the others, so I propose Omar as an initial partner.

I am not comfortable approving Elena and Omar. Elena, I understand your proposal is an initial pairing, but I have a strong concern about Omar that I cannot fully explain yet. On Mission 1, one bad card is enough to fail, so I would rather you revise to a different partner before we vote. Elena, what led you to choose Omar specifically, and would you consider replacing him with Zara?

Omar was an arbitrary initial choice; I had no evidence favoring him over anyone else. I’m willing to consider replacing him with Zara, but I can’t independently verify your concern. Isha, is there a particular reason you prefer Zara as my partner?

Elena, I understand the concern about an arbitrary first pick, but my objection is specifically to Omar. I have a strong reason to distrust Omar that I cannot lay out yet, and Mission 1 has a one-fail threshold, so I cannot vote for any team containing Omar. Zara is not confirmed to me either, but replacing Omar with Zara removes my specific objection and would make the proposal acceptable to me. I am not accusing you; this is about Omar.

I remain opposed to this team because Omar is on it. My concern is specific to Omar, not to Elena. On Mission 1, with a one-fail threshold, I cannot vote for any proposal containing Omar when a safe revision is available. Elena, you said you were willing to consider replacing Omar with Zara; will you revise the team to Elena and Zara now?

Isha, I hear your objection, and I’m considering revising to Elena and Zara. Your concern is not independently verifiable, though, so I don’t want to treat Zara as confirmed Good. Omar, how do you respond to Isha’s specific objection to including you?

Elena, thank you for the chance to respond. Isha, you have now spoken three times about a 'strong concern' regarding me, and in all three statements you have declined to give a single concrete reason. You say you 'cannot fully explain yet,' that you have a reason you 'cannot lay out yet.' That is not evidence; it is an assertion designed to make suspicion feel like information. I have nothing to hide on this team. I am prepared to serve on Mission 1, and a Success card from me will speak for itself when the result is revealed. Notice also the shape of this objection: Isha is not asking you to delay, or to gather more discussion, but to swap in Zara specifically, framing Zara as the 'safe' revision. There is no more evidence for Zara than for me, as Isha herself just admitted when saying Zara 'is not confirmed to me either.' So the proposal on the table is: replace an arbitrary pick with another arbitrary pick, solely to satisfy an unexplained accusation. I do not think the leader should set that precedent on Mission 1. Elena, you were right when you said Isha's concern is not independently verifiable. The one-fail threshold cuts both ways: it makes us careful about who goes, but it also means an unverified claim should not get veto power over every proposal. If we let an unexplained objection dictate the team now, any player will be able to stall every mission this game with the same phrase. My ask is simple: keep the team as proposed, Elena and Omar, and let everyone vote openly. If the table rejects it, so be it, but let that be a judgment on the proposal rather than on an accusation no one can examine.

Omar, your response is fair: I cannot verify Isha’s concern, and Zara is not confirmed Good. Still, the objection is specific enough that I’m considering Elena and Zara rather than dismissing it outright. Zara, how do you assess Isha’s objection and the proposed switch to Elena and Zara?

Elena, thank you for asking my view directly. I will be straightforward: I am willing to serve on Mission 1 if selected, but I want to be clear that I am not a confirmed alternative to Omar — I am simply another unknown at this table, as Isha has already acknowledged. Isha's objection raises concerns on both sides. If Omar truly is Evil, Isha should eventually be able to give the table something concrete to evaluate; repeated vague warnings do not help Good — they only manufacture distrust without accountability. And if the concern turns out to be baseless, Omar has been placed in a defensive position with no way to clear himself. Omar's argument about precedent is well taken: if an unexplained objection can veto any proposal, no mission will ever pass. That said, I am not opposed to Elena revising the team if Elena genuinely believes Elena and Zara is stronger. My point is simply that this switch should not be framed as Omar being removed for cause when no cause has been presented. Whatever team we finalize, I ask that we judge it on the merits rather than on suspicion we cannot examine.

I want to say something that has not been said yet at this table: Isha's objection does not actually change the team, and everyone here seems to have missed that. Elena and Omar, or Elena and Zara — in both cases Omar goes. Isha has framed this as removing Omar, but the proposal on the table is which second player pairs with Elena. If Omar is truly a concern for the table, then a switch to Zara resolves nothing about Omar, it only relabels who Elena trusts. So the honest framing is that Isha wants Elena as a partner and is using an unexamined claim about Omar to shape that outcome.

That framing matters, because it makes the claim unfalsifiable. If Omar goes, Isha's concern was pointless; if Omar stays and the mission succeeds, the concern was baseless; if Omar stays and the mission fails, Isha will say she warned us. No result ever counts against it. Omar has behaved exactly as a loyal player should: asked for a concrete reason, stated his readiness to serve, and accepted the table's judgment. Zara herself, to her credit, said plainly that she is not a confirmed alternative and that she is not being removed for cause. That is a coherent position, and it directly undercuts the idea that this switch is safety.

So I support Elena's original proposal, Elena and Omar, and I would also accept Elena and Zara if Elena genuinely judges it stronger — but on the merits, not on suspicion nobody can examine. Elena, pick the partner you actually believe in.

One last point for whoever is on the team: a Mission 1 result that goes badly is not a disaster, it is information we will never get any other way. If this mission fails, we will learn something real about the table that no amount of talking can produce. I would rather learn it here, early, than repeat the same blind guess on Mission 2 and Mission 3.

Elena, my view has not changed: keep the team as Elena and Omar, and let the table vote on the merits.

Let me put the Isha objection in its strongest form, because I think the table deserves to hear the best version of it and then decide. Isha has made three statements and in none of them has offered a single checkable fact — no claim of a role sight, no odd behavior, nothing anyone else could weigh. What we have instead is a claim that a specific player must be replaced, plus a pre-selected substitute, plus a rationale that changes depending on who is in the room. When the substitute herself says she is not a confirmed alternative and is not being removed for cause, the objective that was supposedly being served disappears. That is not how a serious accusation works; that is how a preference gets dressed up as a concern.

And notice who the concern conveniently excludes. Isha never asked to delay, never asked for more time, never asked anyone to reconsider the whole proposal. She asked for one specific substitution. That means the one player Isha is not willing to pair with Elena is the one player she wants kept off the table, regardless of the reason. On Mission 1, with a single Fail enough to sink us, that is precisely the kind of unexamined influence we should not hand the table — because the cost of being wrong falls entirely on the rest of us.

I want to say clearly that I am not attacking Isha's honesty. She may be reading the table better than I am, and if she has real information she should simply state it, plainly, and let us judge. Vague insistence is not information. If she says something concrete and true, I will accept it immediately and apologize. Until then, we have an arbitrary first pick on one side and an arbitrary swap on the other, and the tiebreak should be the leader's judgment, not an assertion no one can examine. Elena, you proposed a reasonable team, Omar has behaved exactly as a committed player should, and Zara has told us she is no safer than he is. Please keep the team as Elena and Omar and put it to a vote. If the table rejects it, that is a legitimate decision — but it should be made by judgment, not by an accusation we are not permitted to examine.

This is my third and final turn in this discussion, so let me be plain about where I stand and why I am not changing it. I support Elena and Omar. I have said so twice, and I am not going to manufacture a new objection just because the discussion is running long. Let me put the logic of Isha's position in its most charitable form and then show why it still fails. Isha believes Omar is dangerous and wants him off the team. That is a legitimate thing to believe. But the mechanism she has chosen does not test that belief; it circumvents it. She has asked for a swap to a named substitute, not for more time, not for a fuller team, and not for any claim she can articulate. A concern that can only be expressed as 'replace this specific player with this specific other player' is not being weighed by the table — it is being enacted by the table while pretending to be weighed. That is the difference between information and instruction, and it matters on Mission 1 more than any other, because one Fail is enough and the cost of a mistake sits with all of us. I want to be careful here, because I do not think Isha is dishonest. I think she may be reading something real that she cannot yet name. But if that is true, then the fix is not to have her preference ratified by default; the fix is for her to say the thing plainly, in one sentence, and let us judge it. If she gives a concrete claim, I will withdraw my support for Elena and Omar immediately and say so. She has had three turns. She has used them to repeat, in slightly different words, that she has a strong reason she cannot yet lay out. That is now a complete pattern, and a pattern of three turns is evidence of its own: it tells us that the reason will not be arriving this discussion. So the choice in front of us is not 'a safe team against an unsafe one.' Zara has already told us, to her credit, that she is not a confirmed alternative and is not being removed for cause — she is another unknown who happens to be the preferred swap. Swapping would produce Elena and Zara, two people we are equally unable to evaluate, and it would remove Omar on the strength of a claim nobody has examined. That is not a risk reduction. It is a substitution of one blind guess for another, made on the say-so of an accusation we have been told we are not permitted to examine. On the merits, then, and only on the merits: Omar asked for a concrete reason, stated his readiness to serve, accepted the table's judgment without complaint, and made the single best argument anyone has made in this discussion — that letting an unexplained objection dictate teams means no mission in

I have not changed my position, and I want to keep this brief so the table can vote. I support Elena and Omar as proposed.

Isha has now spoken four times, and across all four statements the pattern is identical: a strong concern, an inability to state it, and a pre-selected substitute. Let me be precise about what that pattern means. Isha says she cannot explain her concern 'yet' — but there is no later before this vote. The vote happens now, on the information on the table now, and that information consists entirely of her say-so. If the concern is real, it exists right now, and it could be stated right now. What cannot be stated right now is not a reason to change a team right now.

I also want to name the asymmetry honestly. I am the one being asked to step aside, so everything I say will reasonably be discounted as self-interest. That is fair. But weigh what each of us has actually put forward. Isha has put forward: replace Omar, install Zara, reason unavailable. Zara has put forward, unprompted and at cost to no one: I am not a confirmed alternative, I am not safer than Omar, and this switch should not be treated as removal for cause. That statement cost Zara nothing and gained her nothing — she simply refused to be used as the safe option in a swap she does not believe is justified. That is the most credible testimony in this entire discussion, and it cuts directly against the revision.

Maya laid out the structural problem clearly: Isha's framing is unfalsifiable by design. If the team passes without me, her concern did nothing. If the team passes with me and succeeds, her concern was baseless. If it fails, she claims vindication. There is no outcome that tests her claim. The only test available to this table is to make her say the thing plainly, and she has declined that test three turns running.

Elena, you proposed this team and you have defended the principle that unverified claims should not get veto power. I am asking you to hold to that. I am ready to serve, I will play a Success card, and if this mission fails with me on it, every bit of suspicion I have attracted here becomes legitimate grounds to exclude me from every future team. That is a real stake I am accepting, not an abstract one. Isha risks nothing under her proposal — she simply swaps a name and keeps her assertion intact either way.

Let the table vote on Elena and Omar as proposed, on the merits, with every player's judgment made in the open. If it rejects, I accept that result without complaint — but it should be the table's judgment, not one unexamined instruction being executed.

This is my final turn, so I will keep it short and clear.

The proposal on the table is Elena and Omar, exactly as originally drafted. I support it, and I ask the leader to hold it and put it to a vote.

Nothing in this discussion has changed the facts. Isha has spoken four times and offered no checkable reason to remove me — no observation, no claim about my behavior, nothing anyone at this table can weigh. What has been offered instead is a named substitute, and Zara has told us, plainly and at no benefit to herself, that she is not a confirmed alternative and not a safer option. There is no version of this swap that reduces risk; it only replaces one unknown with another unknown to satisfy an assertion no one has been allowed to examine.

I have stated my position and I stand by it: I am ready to serve, I will play a Success card, and if this mission fails with me on it, everything said here about me becomes fully legitimate grounds to keep me off every future team. I am accepting that stake openly. That is the strongest guarantee I can offer, and it is a real one.

Isha, by contrast, risks nothing under her proposal. Her concern, whatever it is, survives every outcome intact: a success without me proves nothing to her, and a failure would be treated as vindication. A claim that cannot be tested should not dictate who rides on Mission 1 with a one-fail threshold.

Maya and Zara have both made the same core point from different angles: judge the team on its merits, not on an unexamined instruction. Elena proposed this team and defended the right principle — that unverified accusations should not hold veto power over the table. I ask her to stand by that principle now.

I am done speaking. Let the table vote on Elena and Omar, openly, and I will accept the result whatever it is.

I have nothing to add that would change the discussion. I said what I believe on my first turn, and it still holds: I am not a safer alternative to Omar, and removing Omar on the strength of an unexplained claim does not reduce risk — it just replaces one unknown with another. Omar has asked the right questions, Maya has laid out the structural problem clearly, and Isha has had three turns to say something concrete and has not. The leader should hold the team as Elena and Omar and put it to a vote. If the table approves, we play. If the table rejects it, leadership passes and we reconvene with a new proposal — that is what the vote is for. Either outcome is fine. What is not fine is letting a claim nobody can examine quietly decide the team by default. Let us vote.

This is my final turn and my position is unchanged: the table should vote on Elena and Omar as proposed.

Isha, I want to address you directly one last time. I am not accusing you of dishonesty, and I have never been. But across three turns you have offered the same structure — a strong concern about Omar, a pre-selected substitute, and no checkable reason. You have told us you have information you cannot yet lay out. That may be true, but as Omar and Maya have both pointed out, there is no later before this vote. The vote is now.

If you hold a real sight or a concrete observation, this is the moment to state it in plain language so we can evaluate it. I will genuinely weigh whatever you give us. What I cannot do is treat an assertion I cannot examine as a reason to reshape the team.

I have no additional argument to make. The table has heard the full case from every angle. Let us vote on Elena and Omar, openly, and accept the result.
Elena revises the team to Elena, Zara. Isha’s specific concern about Omar may reflect information she cannot safely disclose. Zara is not confirmed Good, but I prefer this revision for Mission 1.
Team approved (4 approve, 1 reject).
Mission 1 succeeds (0 fail cards).

Omar proposes Omar, Zara, Maya. Mission 1 succeeded with Elena and Zara, and Zara also argued fairly throughout the discussion, so she has earned trust on both counts. Isha's unexplained objection to me remains unresolved, and until she offers something concrete I see no reason to hand her a seat while she campaigns against me without evidence. I am including myself as leader to take direct responsibility for this mission, and I will play a Success card.

I will vote against Omar, Zara, Maya. Mission 1 is the only hard result we have: Elena and Zara succeeded with zero fail cards. Replacing Elena with Maya is not a trust-building change. Omar is leading a team that includes himself and Maya, while excluding the player who just completed a successful mission. I opposed Omar in the previous discussion, and nothing since has given me a reason to retract that concern. Maya spent that discussion arguing that my objection should not shape the team, then voted to approve the revised Elena and Zara team anyway; that is not consistency, and it does not make this proposal safer. Zara is the one member of this team I can support, but one good player cannot make a team containing both Omar and Maya safe when a single fail card is enough. I ask Elena and Zara to reject this proposal. I will not support any team containing Omar or Maya unless concrete, checkable evidence changes my assessment.

I will vote against Omar, Zara, Maya. Mission 1 is our only hard result: Elena and Zara succeeded with zero fail cards. This proposal removes Elena, who just completed that mission, and adds both Omar and Maya while keeping Zara. Omar is proposing a team that includes himself and Maya, and Maya spent the previous discussion arguing that my objection to Omar should not shape the team, then approved the revised Elena and Zara team anyway. That is not consistency, and it does not make this proposal safer. Zara is the one member of this team I can support; Mission 1 and her public conduct give me reason to trust her more than either Omar or Maya. But one good member cannot make a team containing both Omar and Maya safe when a single fail card is enough. I ask Elena and Zara to reject this proposal. Nothing since Mission 1 has given me a concrete, checkable reason to retract my concern about Omar, and this team pairs him with another player whose conduct I do not trust. I will not support any team containing Omar or Maya unless concrete, checkable evidence changes my assessment.

I will vote against Omar, Zara, Maya. Mission 1 is the only hard result we have: Elena and Zara succeeded with zero fail cards. This proposal removes Elena, who just completed that mission, and adds Omar and Maya while keeping Zara. Omar is leading a team that includes himself and Maya, while excluding the player who just completed a successful mission. Nothing since Mission 1 has given me a concrete, checkable reason to retract my concern about Omar, and this team pairs him with another player whose conduct I do not trust. Zara is the one member of this team I can support; Mission 1 and her public conduct give me reason to trust her more than either Omar or Maya. But one good member cannot make a team containing both Omar and Maya safe when a single fail card is enough. I ask Elena and Zara to reject this proposal. I will not support any team containing Omar or Maya unless concrete, checkable evidence changes my assessment.

I oppose Omar, Zara, Maya. The successful first mission does not prove Zara is Good, but it gives us more reason to retain Elena and Zara than to replace Elena with two untested players. Isha’s warning about Omar remains unexplained, but I am not comfortable dismissing it, and adding both Omar and Maya increases the uncertainty.

Omar, would you revise the team to Elena, Zara, and Isha, preserving the successful pair and avoiding the players Isha has specifically opposed?

Elena, I appreciate the direct question, but I will not revise to Elena, Zara, and Isha, and I want to explain why plainly. Isha has just announced, in three consecutive statements, that she will vote against any team containing Omar or Maya regardless of composition or merit. Revising to a team that includes Isha means handing a seat on the mission to a player who has pre-committed to opposing me personally no matter what I propose. That is not a coalition I can lead. If Isha had said 'I will support a team that preserves the Elena-Zara pair,' that would be a negotiable position. What she said instead is 'I will not support any team containing Omar or Maya unless concrete, checkable evidence changes my assessment' — and she has simultaneously told us she will never provide the concrete reason that could change it. That is a closed loop. There is no proposal I can make that satisfies it, except one that removes me from leadership and keeps Maya off every future team. I decline to accept that as the standard.

Let me also address the claim that this team excludes the player who just succeeded. Mission 1's result confirms that Elena and Zara played Success cards on a two-person mission. It does not confirm Elena over anyone else, and it certainly does not obligate me, as the new leader, to build every future team around the previous leader. Mission 2 requires three players. Someone who sat out Mission 1 must be added, and Isha has disqualified herself by her own announcement. That leaves me and Maya as the additions, and Maya's record deserves a fair reading: she argued for the original proposal in discussion, and when the leader revised the team, she approved it anyway. That is exactly the behavior of a player who backs the table's judgment rather than her own preference. Isha calls that inconsistency; I call it good faith.

So my position is unchanged: Omar, Zara, Maya stands, and I ask the table to vote it up or down on its merits. If it goes down, leadership passes and someone else can try to assemble a team under Isha's veto rule — and we will all learn something from watching them try. I will play a Success card, and if this mission fails with me on it, I accept that every suspicion raised against me becomes legitimate grounds for my permanent exclusion. That is a real stake, offered openly, against a veto that risks nothing and tests nothing.

I want to put my position on the record plainly, and then I am done arguing. I support Omar, Zara, Maya as proposed. I am on this team, I will play a Success card, and I accept the full stake of that: if this mission fails with me on it, every suspicion that has ever been raised about me becomes legitimate grounds to keep me off every remaining mission. Let me say something I should have said more clearly in the last discussion. Isha's objection has never once been an argument about risk. It has been an instruction: Omar must not be on the team, and Maya must not be on the team, regardless of the composition of the rest of the team and regardless of the merits. That is not a concern the table is weighing. It is a concern the table is executing. And notice what makes it unanswerable: Isha has told us in advance that the only thing that could change her assessment is concrete checkable evidence, and she has told us she will never supply it. So the condition for her support can never be met. That is not caution. That is a veto with a built-in immunity from being wrong. I also want to name something none of us has named. Isha's framing of this proposal as hostile to the successful pair is not accurate. Elena and Zara's success on Mission 1 proves they both played Success cards. It does not make Elena a better candidate than Maya for a three-person mission, and it certainly does not create an obligation to include Elena in every future team. If the standard were 'always keep the last successful pair together,' then no leader would ever have discretion again, and this game would be decided by a single result rather than by judgment. Here is the honest arithmetic of the table as it stands. Five players. Mission 2 needs three. Elena and Zara succeeded together. Isha has disqualified herself by her own repeated announcement — she will not support any team containing Omar or Maya, which on a three-person team rules out nearly every combination she could accept. If the table lets that stand, the only teams that ever reach a vote are the ones Isha has already chosen, and she has chosen one. Then we will discover who the leader is by elimination rather than by leadership. Leadership has to pass to somebody, and when it does, that leader will have no room to maneuver either. I would rather we test a reasonable team now and learn something from the result than spend the rest of this game negotiating with a closed loop. Elena, I will say this to you directly, and I would like your answer before we vote. You were the leader last round and you watched Isha's pattern run for three turns without producing a single checkable reason. Maya, an unexplained claim can matter without being conclusive: Isha may have information she cannot safely disclose. Separately, I know I am Good, and Zara and I succeeded together. That result does not clear Zara, but preserving our pair and adding one player is less uncertain from my perspective than adding both Omar and Maya. I will vote against this team and support Elena, Zara, and Isha instead.

Elena, thank you for stating your position so plainly, because it lets me answer it precisely. You say that preserving your pair with Zara and adding one player is less uncertain than adding both Omar and Maya. But look at what your alternative actually is: Elena, Zara, and Isha. You are not reducing uncertainty — you are swapping me for the one player at this table who has announced, three times, that she will vote against any team containing Omar or Maya before she has even heard the proposal. A player who pre-commits to verdicts regardless of composition is the least predictable addition we could make, and you are proposing to hand her a seat on a mission with a one-fail threshold. That is not caution. That is rewarding the closed loop.

Notice also what your position amounts to as a general rule. If Mission 1 obligates us to keep Elena and Zara together, then that pair must sit on every three-person mission for the rest of the game, and the remaining three of us are competing for a single slot that you effectively control. You proposed on Mission 1, you succeeded on it, and now you vote against the new leader's team while proposing one built to Isha's specification. From where I sit, the pattern is not 'Isha may have information she cannot disclose.' The pattern is that every team must contain Elena, and every objection to that is reframed as uncertainty.

On the record itself: Mission 1 proved that you and Zara played Success cards on a two-person mission. It proved nothing about me or Maya, because neither of us was tested — I volunteered and was swapped out on an unexamined claim. Maya has done nothing but back the table's judgment: she defended the original proposal, approved the revised team anyway, and has now stated openly that she will play a Success card and accept the full stake of a failure. I have made the same stake. Zara served with both of us in discussion and judged fairly then.

So my position is unchanged: Omar, Zara, Maya stands. I will not revise to a team built around Isha's pre-announced veto, and I will not treat one mission result as a permanent entitlement to leadership for its members. I ask every player to vote on the merits of this team: two players who have publicly accepted the stake of failure, and Zara, who succeeded on Mission 1 and has been the fairest voice at this table. If it fails, leadership passes and we proceed. Let the table decide openly.

I have already said most of what I need to say, so I will be brief and put my position on the record again: I support Omar, Zara, Maya, and I am asking the table to vote it up. I am on this team. I will play a Success card. If this mission fails with me on it, then every suspicion ever raised against me becomes legitimate grounds to keep me off every remaining mission, and I accept that stake openly and without complaint. I make the same offer Omar has made. Nobody should be able to say that I sought a seat to avoid exposure.

What I want to add this turn is one thing Isha has never once had to answer, and it is not about whether her concern is sincere. It is about what her standard actually does to the game. Isha has told us she will not support any team containing Omar or Maya, and that the only thing that would change her assessment is concrete checkable evidence she has said she will never supply. A condition for support that can never be met is not a condition; it is a permanent exclusion decided in advance. We are five players, this mission needs three, and on Isha's own rule the only combinations she could ever accept are ones she has already specified. So the practical effect of Isha's position is that leadership does not decide the table. It does not even need to persuade anyone.

I want to be careful here. I am not calling Isha a liar. She may be reading something real that she cannot name, and I would change my mind instantly for one concrete claim. But an unnamed claim cannot be weighed by the table, and Maya and Omar and Zara have each said the same thing from different angles: judge the mission on the merits, not on an assertion we are not permitted to examine. Zara succeeded on Mission 1. Elena succeeded on Mission 1, and nothing since has produced a checkable reason to distrust either of them, yet this proposal excludes Elena on no stated grounds either. I would rather test a reasonable team now and learn something real from the result than negotiate with a closed loop for three more missions.

Omar, do you still want to hold Omar, Zara, Maya exactly as drafted, or do you want to revise after hearing Elena and Isha? Tell me plainly and I will back your call either way.

This is my final turn, so I will be direct. The proposal is Omar, Zara, Maya, and I am holding it exactly as drafted. I will not revise it, and here is why.

The only alternative on the table is Elena, Zara, and Isha — a team built to the specification of a player who has announced, across four consecutive statements, that she will vote against any team containing Omar or Maya no matter what. That is not a negotiating position; it is a closed loop. A claim that can never be supported by evidence, from a player who says she will never supply the evidence, cannot be the foundation of a mission with a one-fail threshold. If we reward that structure now, every future leader inherits it, and every future team is decided by veto rather than by judgment.

Elena has argued that preserving her pair with Zara is less uncertain. I respect her position, but the arithmetic does not support it. Mission 2 requires three players. Elena and Zara succeeded together on a two-person mission, which proves their cards, not their entitlement to every future seat. Someone from Mission 1 must be added, Isha has disqualified herself by her own repeated announcement, and that leaves Maya and me. Maya has publicly accepted the full stake: a Success card from her, and if this mission fails with her on it, permanent grounds for her exclusion. I make the identical stake. If Omar, Zara, Maya fails, then every word said against me here becomes legitimate, and I should never lead or serve again. That is a real wager. Isha's alternative risks nothing and tests nothing.

Zara, you succeeded on Mission 1 and you have been the fairest voice at this table across two discussions. You are on this team as drafted, and you heard the case from every side. I am not asking you to carry my defense; your record speaks for itself, and your judgment on Mission 1 earned you the seat.

To everyone else: I have now spoken my last words on this proposal. My position cannot change, and neither can Isha's, because hers was fixed before the first vote of this mission and mine is fixed by the facts. The table has heard the full argument — Elena's pair-preservation logic, Isha's objection, Maya's stake, and mine. There is nothing left to weigh that discussion can produce. The vote is the only mechanism remaining that generates information, and I welcome it in either direction. If this team passes, we play, and the result will speak. If it fails at the vote, leadership passes, and the next leader will face the same constraint Isha has built: no team containing Omar, no team containing Maya, no evidence ever forthcoming. Let everyone watch how that plays out.

I am ready to serve, I will play a Success card, and I accept the full consequence of failure. Let the table vote on Omar, Zara, Maya, openly and on the merits.

This is my first turn in this discussion, and my position is straightforward: I support Omar, Zara, Maya as proposed, and I will play a Success card if this team is approved.

I want to address Elena directly on the substance of her objection, because it is the only argument at this table that deserves a careful answer rather than a dismissal. Elena, you say preserving your pair with Zara is less uncertain than adding both Omar and Maya. I appreciate that you were willing to say plainly why, but I want to point out that Mission 1's success proves Elena and I both played Success cards on a two-person mission. Avalon supports 5–10 players. Good wins after three successful missions, unless Evil identifies Merlin in the assassination phase. 2. Roles and private information

Merlin is Good and sees Evil players except Mordred. Percival is Good and sees Merlin and Morgana without knowing which is which. Evil players know other Evil players, except Oberon is unknown to the other Evil players and does not know them. The Assassin is an Evil player and makes the final Merlin guess. Loyal Servants know no roles. Agents receive only the private information allowed by their role.

3. Team proposal and approval

The leader proposes a team of the required size and explains their choice. Players discuss the proposed team, and the leader may then keep it or revise it once. Every player votes on the final team. Ballots are revealed together. A strict majority approves; a tie rejects. After a rejection, leadership passes clockwise to a new proposal and discussion. The fifth rejection on the same mission ends the game in Evil’s favor.

4. Mission cards

Only team members submit secret mission cards. Good players must choose Success. Evil players may choose Success or Fail. Normally one Fail card fails the mission. Mission four in games with seven or more players requires at least two Fail cards to fail. Only the mission result and number of Fail cards are revealed; individual cards stay secret.

5. End of game and assassination

Three failed missions give Evil an immediate win. After three successful missions, the Assassin guesses Merlin from among the other players, excluding only their known Evil teammates. If the target is Merlin, Evil wins; otherwise Good wins. There are no further missions after either side reaches its win condition.

6. Discussion and record

Each team proposal is followed by a discussion. Before every speaking turn, the players who still have turns answer a private urgency poll or pass; the most urgent player speaks, with seeded tie-breaking. A speaker may yield the next turn to a player they directly asked a question. Each player has three turns per discussion, including declined turns. When every eligible player passes, the discussion ends. Each statement has at most 500 words. All statements are public. Team proposals, public approval votes, mission outcomes, and the assassination guess are recorded. Private role information, mission cards, and research belief surveys are not shown to other agents.
